reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the speaker promotes a self-deployed Ethereum bot as a source of easy daily passive income and instructs viewers to deposit at least 0.2 ETH into its contract address. The tutorial links larger deposits to greater profit and claims returns of 31% in about twelve hours, with withdrawal presented as returning the deposit plus profit. The frames show contract interaction and a value-bearing MetaMask confirmation, although they do not independently establish that the reported returns were generated or that deposited funds were withdrawn.

citations.quote: Today I will be teaching you step by step how to deploy an Ethereum trading bot I have recently developed in the Solidity language, which can make you very easy daily passive income.
So the next step is to fund a contract with some ethereum to snipe liquidity pools.
But obviously the more you put in, the larger the transactions you will be able to sandwich and the more profit you will be able to sandwich, and the more profit you're able to accumulate over time.
Deposit funds (at least 0.2 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
It takes advantage of decentralized finance platforms such as Uniswap, to sandwich transactions for arbitrage.

opening.argument: Judge, the funding advice is qualified by specific operating costs, not presented as a risk-free threshold. The description discusses gas and possible burn fees, and the speaker says results fluctuate from week to week. Those qualifications matter when weighing the income claims: the video may overstate how attractive the bot is, but it does not present its reported result as a guaranteed return for every viewer.

citations.quote: I've received messages from people who didn't fund the contract with enough Ethereum to cover gas fees and possible burn fees.
If you fund the contract with 0.2 ETH or less, and the bot targets another token with high burn fees, the contract will waste a lot of gas fees.
The province will fluctuate week to week

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening points to a deposit recommendation and claims about higher profits, but neither establishes a fixed or guaranteed payout. The stated reason for the 0.2 ETH recommendation is to account for gas and burn fees. The speaker's own qualification that results fluctuate also limits how the reported return should be read.

citations.quote: I recommend funding the contract with at least 0.2 ETH to make sure that won't happen.
The province will fluctuate week to week

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Cost warnings do not change the central pitch. The speaker invites viewers to deploy a bot for easy daily passive income, directs them to fund its contract, and says larger deposits enable greater profit. The warning about fees even reinforces the recommendation to commit at least 0.2 ETH; it does not substantiate the promised earning mechanism.

citations.quote: Today I will be teaching you step by step how to deploy an Ethereum trading bot I have recently developed in the Solidity language, which can make you very easy daily passive income.
But obviously the more you put in, the larger the transactions you will be able to sandwich and the more profit you will be able to sandwich, and the more profit you're able to accumulate over time.
Deposit funds (at least 0.2 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address

opening.argument: Judge, the video spends substantial time walking through a development workflow: create a Solidity file, inspect an address, choose the matching compiler version, deploy through an injected provider, and use the resulting contract controls. The sampled screens show code, compiler settings, and deployed-contract actions. That is concrete operational instruction, not merely an appeal to send money on the strength of an earnings claim. The reported outcome can be read as the speaker's example within a tutorial, without treating it as an independently verified result.

citations.quote: Under compiler, select the 0.6.6 version so that it matches our contract.
Yep. Perfect. It's the official wrapped Ether address, always a good idea to check that.
Now it's time to check the profits The Bot made for me.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening fairly notes the funding step and the claimed 31% gain, but those points do not erase the demonstrated programming and deployment workflow. Nor do the contract screens independently prove that the claimed gain occurred. They show what the speaker demonstrates; the judge should distinguish that instructional content from verification of the speaker's performance claim.

citations.quote: Now the deployment utility is ready to go, click deploy.
So as you can see I have about 1.31 ETH which is 31% profit already

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The technical walkthrough is the route by which viewers are told to put ETH into the bot. The instructions continue beyond compilation and deployment to funding the contract and starting it, while the speaker promotes the result as easy daily passive income. Showing development tools does not make the funding-and-returns pitch incidental.

citations.quote: After your transaction is confirmed, start the bot by clicking the 'start' button.
Deposit funds (at least 0.2 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
which can make you very easy daily passive income.

opening.argument: Judge, the transaction the speaker asks viewers to make is to a contract they deploy through their own wallet, not, on the cited instructions, a purchase from the speaker or a request for wallet credentials. The description calls it 'your own BOT' after deployment and tells viewers to deposit to their exact contract address. The speaker also describes a withdrawal control. This may be an aggressively promoted trading tool, but a profit claim alone does not show that the creator receives viewers' deposits or controls their wallets.

citations.quote: Move to the 'Deploy' tab, select 'Injected Provider' as the environment, then click 'Deploy'. After the transaction is confirmed, it's your own BOT now
Deposit funds (at least 0.2 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
Withdraw stops the bot and transfers the funds back into your wallet

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening establishes that viewers are encouraged to fund a contract in pursuit of returns. It does not establish who can ultimately receive those funds or that the displayed withdrawal control works as described. The instructions instead describe deployment through the viewer's injected provider and funding the resulting contract address. The earnings claims deserve scrutiny, but these excerpts do not prove diversion of deposits to the speaker.

citations.quote: select 'Injected Provider' as the environment, then click 'Deploy'. After the transaction is confirmed, it's your own BOT now
let's copy the smart contract address to make sure it's created

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it the viewer's bot does not establish who controls the supplied code or where that code can send funds. The video directs viewers to paste externally linked code, deposit ETH, and expect profit from the funded contract. The cited withdrawal description is the speaker's claim, not proof that a viewer can recover a deposit.
